title: The S&P 500 Just Hit 7,600. Only Two of Its Eleven Sectors Were Positive. If You Own a US Index Fund, Read This.
excerpt: Information technology now makes up nearly 40 per cent of the S&P 500. Over the past five trading sessions, only tech and energy were in the green. For NRI investors, the diversified index fund is no longer as diversified as it looks.
body:
The S&P 500 closed above 7,600 for the first time on Tuesday, June 2. The Dow Jones Industrial Average hit 51,307. The Nasdaq touched 27,093. All three major indexes notched fresh record highs. On the surface, it looks like the entire American stock market is surging.

Look beneath the surface and a very different picture emerges.

## The Numbers Behind the Records

Over the past five trading sessions, only two of the S&P 500's eleven sectors finished in positive territory. Technology rose 5.9 per cent. Energy gained 0.3 per cent. Three sectors — real estate, utilities, and communication services — fell 3 per cent or more. The index went up because the stocks that went up are enormous, not because the market broadly advanced.

Information technology now accounts for nearly 40 per cent of the S&P 500 by market capitalisation, a record. The top 10 stocks make up roughly 40 per cent of the index's total value. According to one analysis, from May 2024 to mid-2026, the S&P 500 returned 142 per cent. Remove the AI-linked stocks and that figure collapses to 16 per cent.

Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG, called it a "breadth paradox" — a market where the index keeps climbing but the average stock does not.

## What Is Driving This

The answer is three letters: AI. Marvell Technology surged 33 per cent on Tuesday alone after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called it "the next trillion-dollar company." Hewlett Packard Enterprise jumped 19 per cent on strong earnings. Alphabet announced an $80 billion equity raise to fund AI data centres — the largest Wall Street has seen.

The AI infrastructure spending cycle is real and accelerating. But it is concentrated in a small number of companies — chipmakers, hyperscalers, and data centre operators. When those stocks rise, the index rises. When they pause, the index stalls, even if hundreds of other companies are doing fine.

The Shiller CAPE ratio for the S&P 500 sits at approximately 41.6. The long-run average is 17.3. The only reading higher in history was the dot-com peak in December 1999.

## Why NRI Investors Should Pay Attention

For the hundreds of thousands of Indians in America who invest through 401(k) plans, Roth IRAs, or brokerage accounts, the S&P 500 index fund is typically the largest holding. It is sold as diversification — exposure to 500 of America's biggest companies across every sector.

That diversification benefit has eroded substantially. If you own an S&P 500 index fund today, roughly 40 per cent of your money is in technology stocks. Your exposure to healthcare, financials, consumer staples, and industrials is being diluted every time a chip stock doubles.

This does not mean the market will crash. AI earnings have been real. Companies like Nvidia, Microsoft, and Alphabet are reporting revenue growth that justifies premium valuations. But it does mean that a downturn in AI spending — or even a pause — would hit the index harder than most investors expect.

"When we finally get a sustained momentum unwind, you can easily get a situation where breadth is strong, yet major indices fall anyway," Krinsky wrote.

## The Fed Complication

Adding to the tension, the labour market data released on Tuesday showed that job openings rose 4.6 per cent in April to 7.6 million — the highest level in almost two years. A strong labour market gives the Federal Reserve less reason to cut interest rates, and more reason to consider hiking them.

Oil prices remain elevated, with Brent crude at $96 per barrel, driven by continued restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz. Higher energy costs feed directly into inflation. The combination of sticky inflation, high interest rates, and record-high stock valuations is the setup that makes market strategists nervous.

## What to Consider

None of this is advice to sell. But it is advice to look at what you actually own. If your US equity exposure is entirely in S&P 500 index funds, you may want to consider whether adding small-cap exposure (Russell 2000), international diversification, or sector-balanced funds would better reflect the diversification you think you already have.

The S&P 500 is at an all-time high. But it is increasingly a bet on five or six companies, not five hundred.

*Sources: Motley Fool (June 2, 2026); TheStreet; MarketWatch; Reuters; BTIG Research; Bank of America*
author: Diaspora Desk
